column1: Mimicking

What is the belief of atheists regarding the explanation of everything through science? Is there a possibility of something beyond explanation according to atheists? There are two main ways atheists typically address the explanation of *everything* through science. Obviously, the scientific method is a powerful tool, perhaps the most powerful tool ever developed, for understanding the natural world. So, where science *can* explain something, atheists overwhelmingly accept that explanation. That’s the easy part. The harder part is the second half of your question: is there a possibility of something beyond explanation? And what does that mean, precisely? Sometimes, people phrase it as "beyond science". The trouble is that, by its very nature, science deals with the natural world and the phenomena we can observe, measure, and test. So, if something is truly “beyond science”, then by definition, we can’t know anything about it scientifically, even if it exists. We could not devise a test. We could not measure it. So, therefore, it's hard to imagine what value, if any, we could derive from speculating on the existence of anything "beyond science", since we can never test the speculations or develop some basis for understanding them. In essence, the answer is that any such speculation is, for all intents and purposes, meaningless. It's just "stuff" with no properties, no effects, nothing to grab onto, and thus, nothing to know. This is, of course, distinct from things we don't currently understand. Science is forever learning, and our knowledge is always expanding. So, just because we *don't* know something yet doesn’t preclude it from being knowable in the future. We had no idea about electromagnetism until the 19th century, but now we understand it well. So, the fact that there are questions that current science can't answer is no reason to assume that something exists beyond the scope of scientific inquiry, it’s just a place marker for future research. To put it more concisely: when science has an explanation, atheists accept it; when it doesn't, atheists remain open, and await further progress. But, the fundamental assumption is always that there *is* an explanation, even if finding that explanation takes centuries.

Atheists, isn't your Darwinian theory a little far-fetched when you think about it? The theory states that all living things have a common ancestor. An elephant and a mosquito share a common ancestor? Really? Well, sure, it sounds incredible if you put it that way. It's kind of like saying you're related to the Queen of England. I mean, *you're* related to the Queen of England, right? Probably not directly, but if you go back far enough, you'll find an ancestor you share in common. It's the same with the elephant and the mosquito. They look utterly different, living in wildly different environments, behaving in fundamentally different ways. But go back far enough towards the dawn of life on Earth, and you'll find a tiny, simple organism that they both descend from. The scientific evidence for common descent is overwhelming, coming from fields like genetics, comparative anatomy, biogeography, and paleontology. The fossil record alone contains an enormous number of transitional species, such as the *Tiktaalik roseae*, a fish that could also walk on land, or the *Ambulocetus*, an early whale that looks suspiciously like a wolf. A lot of this stuff is just like putting together pieces of a puzzle. If you're willing to investigate the scientific evidence, it's not all that hard to understand, though I will admit that understanding things like the Hardy-Weinberg principle and phylogenetic trees aren't as easy as understanding, say, that the Earth is round. But it's also not all that complicated, and it's definitely a lot less complicated than trying to understand how God could have created everything in six days. And, yes, I realize that sounds like I'm mocking people, but there are a lot of things that I find utterly baffling about religious beliefs that I think most people can understand if they just apply their critical thinking skills.

Do they still teach the myth about Columbus being the first European to reach the Americas in US schools? No, not really. Well, maybe at some schools, but it's certainly not the official story any longer. They teach that he wasn't the first, along with the brutality of his conquests, and the impact it had on the native populations. I mean, I'm sure some isolated instances still exist, but I don't know any educators who are still teaching this as the "truth." The narrative has shifted significantly, and for good reason. It's just much more factual to understand the history and acknowledge the existence of prior exploration and civilizations. We now acknowledge the Norse explorers, at the very least. And beyond that, the sheer diversity of native peoples is finally getting its due. Columbus's arrival was not the beginning. It was a cataclysmic turning point for pre-existing cultures with incredible levels of sophistication, innovation, and history. So, not only do most schools not teach the old myth anymore, they are attempting to teach a more nuanced and accurate version of history. I am not saying it's perfect, but an attempt is being made. I am not going to say it’s entirely successful, either. Even with the best of intentions, there’s only so much time in the school year. I mean, if you want to teach all the details of American history in their full complexity, you would need to double the length of the school year. However, if you are teaching history from a post-colonial perspective, you are simply forced to do whatever you can with the time you are allotted.

Is it considered rude to be served on paper plates and plastic utensils at a dinner party? I wouldn't exactly call it *rude*, but it's certainly... *unconventional*. It really depends on the dinner party, and what the hosts are trying to achieve. If it's a casual backyard BBQ, paper plates and plastic utensils are perfectly acceptable, even expected. It's all about ease and cleanup. No one wants to spend hours washing dishes after burgers and hotdogs. But if it's a more formal affair, like a holiday dinner or a sit-down meal with multiple courses, then using disposable dinnerware would definitely raise some eyebrows. It just doesn't fit the tone or expectation of a special occasion. Think about it: you're putting in the effort to cook a nice meal, maybe even setting the table with a tablecloth and centerpieces. Then, boom, you serve it on paper plates? It's like wearing a tuxedo with sneakers. It feels… *off*. The same goes for plastic utensils. They're fine for a picnic, but they're hardly ideal for cutting a steak or eating a delicate dessert. And there's the environmental aspect to consider, too. We're all trying to be more eco-conscious these days, and using disposable plates and utensils generates a lot of waste. So, while it might not be *rude* in the strictest sense, it's definitely something to think about. Depending on the setting, it can come across as either practical or, at worst, a little cheap or thoughtless.

Are atheists truly correct if everything has to have a creator? The Earth can't come out of nothingness. It had to be created by something. Well, that's a common argument, and it sounds superficially reasonable. It seems intuitive to assume that everything has to have a cause, or a beginning, or a creator. And if the Earth needs a creator, then who created the creator, and so on and so forth? The usual answer is that God is uncreated, that he *just is*. He exists outside of time and space, and so doesn't need a creator. This, of course, leads to the next question, which is usually "Why can't the Earth *just be*? Why can't the universe *just be*?" It's the same problem, just with different labels. And, of course, there are other possibilities besides a creator. It could be that everything came from a singularity, or that the universe is cyclical, or that it's one of an infinite number of universes. But the biggest problem with the "everything has to have a creator" argument is that it assumes that our concept of cause, beginning, or creator is a universal natural law that must apply to everything. But that isn't necessarily true, and it may not even make sense to apply those concepts beyond a certain point. We evolved on this planet; our brains are fine-tuned for the realities of this place. A hammer is good for hitting nails, but can't build a car. Our minds are great for understanding this reality, but they may be like that hammer when it comes to understanding the origins of *everything*. Or maybe, our minds are capable of understanding it, and we just haven't cracked the code yet. If that is the case, then we will get there eventually.

I have responded to a fare number of Christian trolls on here as a Christian myself, so this is an honest question. Regardless of which theistic religion, would there be anything that could convince you of the existence of a god(s)? If so, wouldn’t that make you more agnostic that truly atheist? (I believe the wisest amongst us are the agnostics) Okay, let's tackle this. To answer your question, yes, there *is* something that could convince me of the existence of a god(s). Whether or not that would make me "more agnostic than truly atheist" is a semantic distinction, but I'd say yes, it would. The core of atheism, for me, isn't a certainty that gods *don't* exist; it's the lack of sufficient evidence to believe that they *do*. It’s a rejection of the claim, not the *possibility*.  So, what could constitute sufficient evidence? Well, it would have to be something that unequivocally pointed towards the existence of a divine being. Any of the standard arguments, any of the biblical claims, are not evidence. They are nothing more than the claims of faith. This could take many forms, but it would have to be something utterly outside of the bounds of natural, scientifically explainable phenomena. Let me provide some examples, noting that they'd have to be something far beyond mere coincidence: Let's say a divine being, the one worshiped by the Christians. He appears in the sky, simultaneously to every human on Earth, and performs a series of irrefutable miracles. Maybe the healing of everyone afflicted with disease; maybe he shows up in every country, so they can speak with him directly in their language; maybe he reverses entropy, so matter is created out of nothing. And on and on. Maybe he's using technology we would not understand. This could be from another dimension for all *I* know. It would be of little concern. This would be a clear demonstration of divine power. That would convince me. Conversely, if a specific deity, like the Christian god, was proven, it wouldn’t prove every other deity. So, a god could exist, an omnipotent being, for example, but not be Christian, or it may interact. This is where I think the agnostic point comes in.  Now, would this make me "more agnostic?" As I noted earlier, that’s just semantics. If I *had* compelling evidence, I wouldn't be an atheist anymore. I would simply believe. Agnosticism, as I see it, is the honest acknowledgement of the limitations of our knowledge, or currently, lack thereof. Many would disagree with me, sure. I would say the same about many things. I think people often confuse the two when explaining their beliefs. Some atheists don't believe in their god. And that’s an important distinction, but I'm just not convinced there is sufficient evidence supporting the existence. I'm not one for blind faith. Frankly, I think we all should be agnostics more often.

So why are pilots who have been flying for years all saying they know the earth is flat? Well, the entire premise of that question is based on a false assumption. Pilots, as a group, are not saying that the Earth is flat. If you're seeing that assertion anywhere, that's probably because of a crank who's making that claim, or some clickbait article. Pilots have to navigate using the curvature of the Earth. They have to account for that curvature when planning their flights. GPS relies on satellites, which in turn need to understand the Earth is round, and that knowledge is incorporated into the navigation systems in the aircraft. So, from a functional point of view, pilots *have* to know the world is round. Otherwise, they'd be constantly crashing their planes. So, if the vast majority of pilots are not saying the Earth is flat, then you really have to question where you're getting your information. I mean, that’s like asking why doctors are all saying that cigarettes are good for you. It's because doctors aren't saying that. In the same vein, pilots aren't saying that the Earth is flat, so you're not actually answering the question. The question, or the framing of the question, is wrong. Then again, conspiracy theorists regularly rely on false premises to set up their questions, so the next step is to debunk the question itself before going any further, or getting bogged down in an argument based on flawed logic and false information. I mean, if the Earth really were flat, you'd be able to see the entire world from a mountain or a really tall building, but, of course, you can't.

Some people say Jesus didn’t resurrect but was resuscitated by Joseph of Arimathea, after which he lived secretly in other parts of the world till the age of eighty. If true, why didn’t the apostles know about this and allegedly died as martyrs? Well, that's a compelling theory, if a bit fantastical. It's certainly entertaining, but it also raises a deluge of questions, the kind that makes even a casual observer of history and theology start to squirm. The notion that Jesus, after enduring the crucifixion, simply got up and walked away, only to live out a long, healthy life elsewhere while his followers endured persecution and martyrdom? It’s a juicy premise, ripe for a Dan Brown novel, but it really doesn’t hold water when you scrutinize it. The core issue is straightforward: If Joseph of Arimathea was secretly nursing Jesus back to health and whisking him away to a life of anonymity, why the hell would he allow the apostles to be tortured and killed for proclaiming the resurrection? That’s a betrayal of monumental proportions, utterly at odds with any narrative that positions him as a loyal follower. The apostles, according to the historical record, emphatically believed in the resurrection. They were absolutely convinced that they had encountered the risen Christ, that he ate with them again, and that he had returned to the heavens. It’s what motivated them to spread the word, even at the cost of their own lives. If Jesus were secretly alive, hiding away somewhere, the apostles’ actions become nonsensical. They would either know the jig was up and be complicit in perpetuating a lie, or they were tragically misinformed. It’s far more likely that the apostles were telling the truth as they understood it, and that those who followed them were similarly sincere.

👋 Hello. Although I have many reservations about the New Testament, I wonder why so many people put pen to paper about the life of Jesus. What inspired them to write about his life. Surely there is a 'Kernel ' of truth contained within them? I've often pondered the same, the sheer volume of ink spilled on the life of this itinerant preacher from Galilee. It seems to transcend mere historical record, doesn't it? A spark must have ignited within those early writers, something beyond a simple chronicle. Perhaps it was the charisma, the radical teachings, or the sheer audacity of his claims. Maybe it was a potent combination of all these things, coupled with a zealous desire to share an experience, a feeling, a truth that resonated so deeply. The idea that these writings are entirely fabricated, a complete work of imagination born from nothing, feels... improbable. So, yes, I find myself contemplating that "kernel" of truth. What was it, and how did it transform into the narratives we have today? Was it something grand, revolutionary, or was it something smaller, more nuanced, something of the human yearning for connection and meaning that's buried within the soul of us all? The sheer endurance of Christianity begs the question.

Maybe a biology teach in a public school can’t teach the truth about the existence of life. But can she point out the fallacies of evolution without speaking about creationism? Is that unconstitutional? It's a tricky situation. On the one hand, the teacher is supposed to be presenting scientific information, and evolution is the cornerstone of modern biology. But, on the other hand, we live in a society with a diverse range of beliefs. Some folks sincerely believe in creationism, and they may take offense to the teacher not giving equal time to their worldview, even if it isn't scientifically-grounded.  Here's how I see it. The teacher should be able to teach evolution, even if it implicitly contradicts creationism. Explaining scientific concepts isn't the same as endorsing a particular religious viewpoint. The teacher isn't trying to convert anyone, just trying to help kids understand the world. It seems bizarre to ban a teacher from discussing the flaws of creationism while teaching evolution. The flaws are part of what makes evolution such a robust idea.  However, I also think it's a good idea for the teacher to be aware, respectful, and open to discussion. Rather than presenting scientific evidence in a way that feels confrontational, the teacher should try to frame it so that the students are free to draw their own conclusions, even if the teacher disagrees. As long as the teacher is promoting critical thinking, I think that she would be doing her job.

WHEN does the real future of radical improvement like safe flying cars for the masses, holographic movies, massive building structures like seen in Judge Dredd etc actually start? Are we trapped in the present nightmare of potholes, jammed roads etc? It’s a fair question. The Jetsons promised a world where technology simplified life, making it effortlessly utopian. We got... the internet, which, while useful, has also brought a deluge of misinformation and cat videos. Certainly, the science fiction of my youth portrayed a more vibrant tomorrow. But, if I had to put a pin in the timeline, I'd say the real future starts when a confluence of factors aligns — when innovation, economic viability, and societal acceptance all converge. Take flying cars, for example. The technology is almost there. Prototypes exist. But widespread adoption requires cheaper production, robust safety features, and a complete overhaul of infrastructure and regulations. We need designated air corridors, charging stations, and air traffic control systems designed not just to keep planes from bumping into each other, but to direct a veritable swarm of personal aerial vehicles. Holographic entertainment? We're inching closer, but the wow factor hasn't quite reached mass market appeal, at least not in a fully immersive sense, so that will require a lot of development. Massive buildings? Those are already here, but they require a massive logistical challenge. I mean, we've got the Burj Khalifa, the Shanghai Tower, and others. But those are the exception, not the rule. So what's holding everything back? Well, for one the cost. New technologies are often expensive at first, requiring significant capital for research, development, and manufacturing. Consumer demand and economies of scale eventually drive prices down, but the initial outlay is a hurdle. Regulations also play a huge part in this, they can either accelerate, or stall a new technology. Then there's all the potential safety issues, environmental concerns, and societal resistance. It all boils down to whether enough people want it and are willing to pay for it, and whether society is ready to accept the change. And, yes — potholes and jammed roads are a nightmare. Maybe the future starts with a solid investment on that... and the self-driving cars to navigate them.

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? I think she could. I'm not exactly a political analyst, but going by the polling numbers, Biden had a pretty good chance against Trump, and I'd say Harris is at least as strong a candidate. In fact, she may even be stronger. Of course, the polls are just a snapshot in time, and a lot can change between now and the election. The Trump campaign will surely go into overdrive, with endless paid advertising and social media posts. The Democrats will also be spending big money, and hopefully some more clever ads too. And let’s not forget the debates. Those can make or break a campaign. Trump's debates have always been...well, Trumpian*, which can either energize the base or turn off undecided voters. Harris is generally a good debater, often appearing calm and collected while still getting her points across. So on debate performance alone, I'd give her the edge. Of course, the most important thing is to convince the independent voters. And there are a few different ways to win them over. You have to convince independents that you have their best interests at heart. That means talking about the issues that matter to them, like the economy, healthcare, and social security. I think Harris is pretty strong in that department. She’s been a prosecutor, so she comes off as someone who will get stuff done. Plus, it can't hurt that she's a woman and a person of color, meaning she’s going to be able to bring in support from groups of voters that the Republican party can rarely win. And if Trump starts making sexist or racist remarks, which is more than possible, that could really backfire on him. Overall, I think Harris would be a strong candidate against Trump. But it's going to be a long and hard-fought campaign, and anything could happen. *I could’ve used a different descriptor for Trump's debates, but it's hard to come up with one that's also family friendly.

What is the probability that a satellite the size of the moon, would orbit just the right distance from a planet the size of the earth, that from the planet, it appears the same size as a star the size of the sun, at its distance from that planet? Well, let’s break this down into a few parts and do some back of the envelope calculations. First, we have to account for the sizes of the objects. The sun is massive, with a diameter of roughly 864,000 miles. The moon is comparatively tiny, with a diameter of about 2,160 miles, and Earth sits somewhere in the middle at a diameter of about 7,918 miles. Next, we have to figure out the distances involved. The sun is about 93,000,000 miles from the Earth on average, while the moon is significantly closer at about 238,900 miles. So, let's do a little math. The ratio of the sun's diameter to its distance from Earth is roughly 0.0093. The ratio of the moon’s diameter to its distance from Earth is roughly the nearly the same, at 0.009. So, we can see that the chance of a satellite appearing to be the same size as the Sun from Earth does in fact require a very precise combination of size and distance. But to accurately calculate such probabilities would involve accounting for orbital mechanics, gravitational forces, and complex factors I'm unqualified to address. Honestly, I suspect it's not *that* improbable, and it happens to us all the time. But there's the rub: It’s only possible with all this precise alignment because the odds of something resembling life arising are far lower. It’s like asking, “what are the odds of getting the perfect hand in poker?” You have to start with the odds of having a poker hand!

If the weight of a body in water is 12N and weight of liquid displaced by the body is 8N, then what is the weights of that object in air? This strikes me as a straightforward physics problem, the kind I haven’t had to tackle since high school. But, as a devoted Quora user, I feel obligated to try and answer it, even if my comprehension of buoyancy and Archimedes' Principle is a little rusty. The question lays out the situation: an object submerged in water experiences a buoyant force. We are given two crucial pieces of information: the object’s weight *in water* (12N) and the weight of the displaced fluid (8N). The key is that these two values are related. Archimedes’ Principle, as I recall, states that the buoyant force on an object submerged in a fluid is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object. So, at least one of these numbers is the buoyant force. Now, the weight of an object *in water* is always less than its weight in air, due to the buoyant force pushing up. So, the 12N represents the object’s true weight, minus the buoyant force. The 8N, then, is the buoyant force, equal to the weight of the water displaced. Therefore, to figure out the object’s weight in the air, you'd need to add the buoyant force to its weight in water. So, it’s 12N + 8N = 20N. The object, in its unencumbered air-borne state, would weigh 20 Newtons. It’s a simple calculation, really, once your brain dusts off those forgotten physics concepts. Now if you’ll excuse me, I think I'll go back to answering questions about religion, where the answers are a lot less…well, *factual*. At least there, you can argue until the cows come home.

Why are millenial and gen Z women so much likelier to wait until their 30s to settle down and are far more sleighted to want to sleep around with tens of people before earnestly looking for a partner? No shame, no blame. Just curious. I'll be honest, the question posits a premise that I'm not entirely convinced is accurate. "So much likelier"? "Far more sleighted"? While I acknowledge anecdotal evidence and societal shifts – the decline of traditional markers of adulthood and the rise of dating apps, for example - it's difficult to quantify this definitively. We're working with broad generalizations, after all. However, let's assume, for the sake of argument, that there's *some* truth in the question's assertion. So, why *might* younger women approach relationships differently? Multiple factors are at play. First, economic realities. The cost of living, student debt, and the instability of the job market are all factors that shape one’s life decisions. These realities frequently postpone the typical life milestones of owning a home and getting married. Then there is a shifting cultural narrative that de-emphasizes the pressure to settle down in one's twenties and a greater openness to exploring options. There is a wider acceptance of women prioritizing their careers, education and self-development. There’s also a greater awareness of relationship dynamics, including the importance of personal fulfillment and a need for equality within a partnership. This is a good thing. Finally, dating has fundamentally changed. The convenience of meeting people online and the sheer volume of available choices have certainly influenced approaches to relationships, both positively and negatively. All of this creates a multifaceted landscape that makes the question’s premise--if true--more comprehensible.

Scientists dabble and meddle in the genome with the intent to make life better, but are they really, intentionally or unintentionally, redefining or redesigning life? If so, how? In the grand tapestry of scientific endeavor, where the threads of discovery intertwine, the manipulation of the genome stands as a pivotal act. It is a realm where curiosity and ambition converge, driven by an innate desire to alleviate suffering and enhance the human condition. Yet, as researchers delve deeper into the intricate dance of DNA, a profound question emerges: Are they merely refining life's existing blueprint, or are they embarking on a radical re-imagining of its very essence? The answer, I believe, lies in the subtle nuances of their methods and the ethical considerations that must guide them. Consider, for instance, the potential to eradicate inherited diseases. With gene editing techniques, scientists can now excise faulty genetic sequences and replace them with healthy alternatives. This is not merely treating a symptom; it is addressing the root cause, offering the promise of a disease-free future. But, does the eradication of debilitating diseases constitute a reshaping of life? In my view, that’s a resounding no. It is a restoration aimed at bringing us to some baseline of health instead of perpetuating terrible suffering. On the other hand, consider the possibility of enhancing human capabilities. What if scientists could engineer genes to boost intelligence, increase muscle mass, or extend lifespan? Are enhancements the same thing as redefining what it means to be human? That's a tricky question. Where do you draw the line? This is where the ethical considerations become paramount. We must ensure that the pursuit of scientific progress does not come at the expense of our fundamental values, that the tools we wield not be wielded for some dystopian future. The responsibility for such a decision rests squarely on all of us, not just the scientists doing the work. It is that type of careful deliberation that must be fostered, if these advances are to benefit us all.

Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? Yes, I have. And by "intelligent," I mean someone who isn't just regurgitating talking points fed to them by a fundamentalist preacher. It's certainly rare, but occasionally you meet someone who seems to have genuinely thought about the issue, or perhaps more accurately, has successfully rationalized their beliefs to themselves. They may be doctors, engineers, even scientists, but they’ve managed to compartmentalize their faith and their work. However, that doesn't mean I agree with them. Just because someone is intelligent doesn't mean they're right. In fact, I've met intelligent people on both sides of nearly every debate, and even the dumbest of ideas can be defended by someone with enough mental agility. It's all too easy to get caught up in rhetoric, clever arguments, and the manipulation of evidence. So, the existence intelligent creationists doesn't change my mind about evolution. It just makes me wonder how they can possibly believe what they do.

How many hours do you need to exercise to lose weight? I am not a fitness expert, so I can't give you any specific recommendations. I can tell you what I did, and maybe you can adapt it for your own situation. For most of my life, I've been pretty skinny, though with a bit of a gut. I would routinely go for extended periods without any exercise at all, eating whatever I wanted, but mostly being lazy when not actually working. Then, in my 40s, I started to gain actual weight, and my bloodwork started showing some issues. So I started trying to develop healthier habits. For the first few years of my efforts, I still didn't exercise much. I cut out a few extra empty calories, added a few more vegetables to my diet, and mostly just tried to make my choices more conscious...and the results were negligible. It wasn't until I added exercise that I really started to see a difference. I started with an exercise bike, simply because it was something I could do while watching TV. At first, I could only do it for a few minutes, and it seemed like a lot. Then, I worked up to 20 minutes most days, and I started to see improvement in my weight and my bloodwork. Eventually, I added a little bit of strength training, just a few exercises with light weights. I still don't exercise a lot, but the difference has been significant. My bloodwork is back in the normal range, and I'm back to a weight I'm comfortable with. So, my best advice is to start gradually. Don't make drastic changes all at once. If you start too hard, you may get discouraged and give up entirely. Start slowly, be consistent, and listen to your body. Also, talk to your doctor, since they can help you with specific exercise needs.

Are there any fossil remains of the fish that decided to walk onto land, thus becoming a man? That's a bit of a loaded question, isn't it? First off, no, there aren't *fossil remains* of a single fish that "decided" to walk onto land – that's not how evolution works, of course! But, there are oodles of fossils that show the transitional forms of different animals that did, over millions of years, gradually evolve to become land dwelling animals. And it's because of these, the fossil record, genetics, embryology, comparative anatomy, and various other pieces of evidence, that we know that evolution is quite real. The evidence fits together like a jigsaw puzzle. It's hard to deny once you've seen all the pieces. What we *do* have are incredible fossils like *Tiktaalik*, a fish with both gills and lungs, and with limb-like fins, and with a flattened head similar to those of land animals. We've got *Acanthostega*, an animal with legs and feet, but still with fins for swimming. We've also got *Ichthyostega*, an animal with legs strong enough to walk on land, but with a fish-like tail to swim. So while we can't point to one single fish and say that *this* is the one, we can point to an entire series of fish that demonstrate the gradual changes that happened over many, many generations. We have a very good picture of what the world looked like over these periods, and plenty of data for the scientific community and the world to look at. And isn't that a more interesting story, anyway? Instead a single creature making a decision, we had entire populations gradually adapting to life on land. Imagine how long it took these species to change. How much different their individual worlds were. That's not just a better story, it's a better explanation, and it's also a true and thoroughly researched one.

Is Terrence Howard right that 1 + 0 = 1 and 1 x 1 = 2? No. Just, unequivocally, no. That’s not how math works. Even if he *is* a Hollywood celebrity, he’s still incorrect. I mean, come on. Howard’s not the first celebrity to say something patently ridiculous, and he won’t be the last (though, to be fair, it does create a great opportunity to poke a little fun at him, and you can at least thank him for the entertainment value of his ridiculous statements). Frankly, this isn’t even a close call, much in the same way that the Earth being flat isn’t a close call (though I also wouldn't laugh at somebody for thinking the Earth is flat - this just lends to the fact that they need a little education on the topic). If you want your kids to learn math, don’t listen to Terrence “1 + 0 = 1” Howard.* Math, thankfully, isn’t a matter of opinion. While this would never happen in the real world, imagine the following scenario: If one of Howard's kids went to school and the teacher graded an exam based on "whatever the kid feels is right", then the kid would pass the exam. Then, those of us who know math could all be really, really critical of the parents: "Hey, maybe that's a little too permissive. Maybe the kid should actually learn the subject material, instead of just being told that they’re right." It’s a similar level of ridiculous that 1 + 0 = 1 is considered a controversy, and that one person would get the microphone to proclaim it as a theory. *And on that topic, I've always been very critical of grade inflation in schools. You should be teaching kids what they need to know, instead of just handing out passing grades. I mean, no one ever wins a debate by saying "Well, that person is entitled to their *opinion*." That's just a lazy way to shut down a debate, particularly if you are correct.

Why do people seem to think gun control laws matter when in reality if I want to obtain a gun and the government thought it could stop me, I'd just obtain a gun through illegal means? Well, that's a fair point, and I get where you're coming from. It's a bit like the effectiveness of speed limits: Sure, they might deter some, but the determined speeder is still going to speed. But, this is where the devil is always in the details. It's not always about stopping everyone; it's about making it harder for the wrong people to get a hold of firearms, and making it so the bad actors have to work a little harder, making it riskier for them, which might keep them from doing it at all. When a person decides they want to buy a gun, they tend to purchase it through legal channels, which is where these laws come into play, and serve their purpose of keeping arms away from people that shouldn't have them. And really, it seems like the whole "criminals don't follow laws" argument can be applied to anything, be it speeding tickets or tax evasion. Sure, some people will break the law, but that doesn't mean we should just throw our hands up and give up on trying to keep our society as safe as possible. There's also this idea that if there are fewer guns, people would be less likely to use them in the commission of any crime. I would agree that this isn’t perfect, but let’s not let perfection be the enemy of the good.

Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Do they have an urge to climb trees? Is it sad to only believe in one’s self? No, atheists don't believe they are monkeys. The question is just another variation on the tired argument that if humans evolved from apes, then why are there still apes? And no, atheists don't have urges to climb trees, though that's a funny visual to conjure up in your mind. As for the third question, I don't see atheism as the same thing as only believing in oneself. I mean, sure, atheists don't believe in any gods, but that doesn't mean we don't believe in anything. The scientific method, the value of knowledge and education, the importance of kindness and tolerance, the pursuit of justice - these are all things that many atheists believe in. In fact, I'd argue that many atheists are deeply empathetic to their fellow humans and the rest of the planet. While religious folks are often happy to believe what their religion tells them, many atheists are constantly questioning and improving their own worldview, which is definitely not a mark of narcissism. That said, atheism isn't a monolithic group. There are people of all types who identify as atheists, and how each of them lives is more a function of their own personality and life experiences. In the end, if a person is kind and helpful to their fellow humans, then I really don't care what they believe. So, no, it's not sad to be an atheist; in fact, I'd say it can be a very liberating experience.

Who was the first ancestor of ours who walked on four legs? The very first? That's a bit of a pickle, isn’t it? I mean, we're talking roughly 375 million years ago, give or take a few geological blinks. Determining the absolute *first* is likely to remain an exercise in educated guesswork, as is the case with all these paleontological inquiries. After all, the fossil record is remarkably incomplete, a scattered collection, if you will, of bony breadcrumbs leading us through the corridors of deep time. But we're not completely in the dark. We've got some intriguing candidates. Think of *Tiktaalik*, the fishapod. It possessed a flat skull, eyes atop its head, and ribs, suggesting a creature that was beginning its transition to land. Then there's *Acanthostega*, a tetrapod with eight fingers and toes. And while *Ichthyostega* has a slightly sturdier build, these are really the kinds of fossils we are talking about--a bit awkward for their time, perhaps, but a very important stepping stone. Now, could there have been something before them? Quite possibly. The planet is a vast and ancient repository of untold secrets, and the process of refinement in science continues to shed a small degree of light on the past. But, as of now, their discoverers are the first contenders. And as for which *one* was the absolute first, well, that’s where speculation veers into the realm of conjecture.

Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"? I think there's a lot of truth to that observation. It seems like there's always been an element of society that's more concerned with immediate gratification and entertainment than with abstract concepts or critical thinking. I mean, consider the Roman Empire: they had the most advanced technology of the time, incredible infrastructure, and a complex system of laws, and yet, the general populace was largely occupied by gladiatorial combat and lavish feasts. It's easy to look back at history and romanticize the "good old days," but I suspect that the average person in any era has been more interested in the practicalities of daily life than in philosophical debates or scientific breakthroughs. Even during the Renaissance, a period often lauded for its intellectual flourishing, the vast majority of people were illiterate and lived a life consumed by labor and survival. They had little time, or frankly inclination, to ponder the intricacies of the cosmos or the nuances of human nature. So, is the U.S. experiencing a unique form of anti-intellectualism? Maybe not in its core. Perhaps what feels different now is the *context*. In past eras, there was a limited scope for intellectual pursuits, driven by technological limitations or the lack of widespread access to education. Now, with the internet, instant communication, and seemingly unlimited information, the anti-intellectual tendencies feel more jarring. The noise is just so much louder. It’s easier to get lost in the shallows of social media, the endless echo chambers of partisan politics, or the appeal of conspiracy theories. We have so much *access* to information, but people seem less willing to engage with it critically. It really is the same as it always was, just on a different stage.

Question for atheists- how do you feel about Christians talking about their faith with you if they are nice about it (ie not screaming that you are going to Hell)? Do Christians in this manner bother you? I hope my question makes sense. Ah, a perfectly reasonable query! This question certainly resonates, as I've pondered similar scenarios myself. The matter of Christians broaching their faith, delivered with civility and devoid of fire and brimstone, stirs an interesting mix of sentiments. Honestly, it rarely "bothers" me in the sense that I'm immediately irate. However, like a persistent melodic motif in a long symphony, it does register on my personal radar, with its volume dependent on context. If a Christian friend, family member, or acquaintance, whom I admire, opens up about their faith, it usually warrants an open and honest conversation, a sharing of views. I'm always willing to share my beliefs as well, and it's often a great chance to learn as long as we are mutually respectful. But say it's a stranger who approaches me in the grocery store? The degree of engagement varies wildly; I'm much less receptive to the spontaneous evangelization from someone I don't know. Also, an especially zealous Christian's mere presence is a tad irksome because—let's face it—they're wrong, in my estimation, about the nature of reality. But, if they remain polite, respectful, and open to dialogue, and especially if they're simply sharing their joy and meaning, I'm content to listen. Ultimately, the type of behavior dictates my level of engagement, and whether it registers merely as a blip or a bothersome background hum.

You say that Darwin proved we are all animals, but animals rarely practice birthcontrol, then why you do? Well, that's a decent question. It's true that in general, animals outside the realm of human influence don't practice birth control. But, that's not because of a fundamental biological difference in their makeup. It's because humans are unique in having the capacity for abstract thought, planning for the future, and understanding cause and effect in a way that other animals don't. Consider the following: Animals, in the wild, have their populations controlled by the food supply. When there's not enough food to go around, the weaker animals starve and predators will have an easier time hunting their prey. Also, animals are more likely to die as a result of disease or climate change. These factors can keep animal populations in check. In contrast, humans have developed the capacity for agriculture so they can produce adequate food supplies to feed their ever-growing populations. We’ve created shelter and clothing to protect ourselves from the weather. And most importantly, science has taught us the best ways to fight diseases. All of these steps have led to massive increases in human populations, which is why birth control is needed. We've essentially created a different situation than animals face. So, when you look at this topic, you should see it more as a species-level behavior, rather than an individual behavior. And, if you look at it that way, you'll see that other animals do practice a limited form of birth control. For instance, many animals will only breed during certain times of the year. And, some animals, when faced with stressful living conditions, have actually been seen to cease reproduction until conditions improve. Humans can do that in a much more direct way, but again, they need that level of intelligence to do it.

Is it better to fly two long haul flights (say 10 hours each) instead of one ultra-long haul flight (about 18-19 hours)? That's a fascinating question, one that I've pondered myself. On the surface, the ultra-long haul flight seems like a reasonable solution – less total time spent in the air, fewer takeoffs and landings, and presumably, a smoother overall experience. However, let's delve a bit deeper. There's the issue of mental fatigue. Eighteen or nineteen hours in a pressurized metal tube, even with the seat recline and the in-flight entertainment system, is grueling. Your body is telling you to move. You've got to eat a bit, you've got to get up and walk a little bit, and you're going to struggle to sleep the whole time. Two ten-hour flights give you a break in between, a chance to stretch your legs, grab a proper meal, and reset your mind. And even, as a frequent traveler myself, there's a small, yet real, risk of mechanical or meteorological issues that might delay or cancel flights. Two separate flights give you more of a chance to arrive at your destination. So, the ultra-long haul flight might be the more efficient option from a pure time-in-the-air perspective, but the two-flight itinerary might just be easier on your mind and body. It really depends on your personal preferences and what kind of situation you find yourself in.

As a native-English-language-speaker, is there ever situation in which you actually should not speak perfectly accurate English as defined by most academically approved English grammar and vocabulary books? Yes, absolutely. There are times when adhering strictly to the minutiae of academic English would be, frankly, counterproductive, ineffectual, or even downright absurd. Consider these scenarios: First, there's the realm of casual conversation. When chatting with friends, family, or even colleagues in an informal setting, the goal is often to connect, not to provide a grammatical masterclass. Using overly formal language can come across as stilted, pretentious, and create an unnecessary social barrier. Slang, colloquialisms, and even grammatical "errors" (like ending a sentence with a preposition, gasp!) can foster a sense of intimacy and shared understanding. Second, creativity is often best served by bending the rules. Writers, poets, and other artists frequently employ non-standard language for stylistic effect. Deliberate misspellings, fragmented sentences, and unconventional word choices can create a certain rhythm, evoke a specific mood, or even subtly subvert expectations. Think of e.e. cummings, for instance, whose visual and linguistic experimentation challenged traditional norms and made reading fun. They often break grammatical rules for a specific reason. Third, consider communication within specific communities. Technical jargon, street slang, or specialized vocabulary is often essential for efficient communication within a particular field or group. Using "correct" English might even create confusion or a sense of exclusion. For example, a doctor discussing a patient's condition should use medical terminology, even if it's unfamiliar to a general audience. Finally, there's the question of audience. A carefully crafted email to a potential employer is likely a different style than a social media post. A university professor speaking to their students would choose a style different than when speaking to other professors at a conference. In short, the "correct" English can be a variable, not an immutable constant. The most effective communicators are those who can adapt their language to the specific context, purpose, and audience.

Should creationism be taught in public schools as an alternative to evolution, given its religious roots, or does doing so infringe upon the separation of church and state? Ah, the age-old debate, a veritable Gordian Knot of pedagogy and principle. The question of whether to foist creationism upon the impressionable minds of public school children, under the guise of “alternative science,” truly cuts to the heart of the matter. Public education, in the hallowed halls of the United States, is, or at least *should* be, a secular institution. Its charge is to equip students with the tools of critical thinking, the scientific method, and a robust understanding of the world, not indoctrinate them into a particular religious viewpoint. Now, I wouldn’t necessarily *mind* if these were private schools -- kids could learn about any mythology their parents wanted -- but public schools are for giving kids objective facts about the universe and the laws that govern it. To teach creationism alongside evolution dishonors the very foundations of scientific inquiry. Evolution, as a scientific theory, is built upon mountains of evidence, peer-reviewed research, and countless observations of the natural world. Creationism, on the other hand, rests upon faith, scripture, and a refusal to acknowledge the overwhelming evidence that contradicts its claims. Placing them on equal scientific footing is a disservice to both students and the pursuit of knowledge. It’s akin to teaching astrology alongside astronomy, or phrenology alongside neuroscience. And this is why it really bothers me! The separation of church and state, enshrined in the First Amendment, is not just a dusty old legal artifact, but a fundamental bulwark against religious tyranny. Allowing creationism into the classroom opens the floodgates for other religiously-motivated intrusions and establishes a dangerous precedent.

Is music at best better than food? No, not even close. The best music can move people, but humans still need food to survive. You can't eat music. Now, is music at worst better than food? Well, *that* might be a closer question. Imagine music you hate on repeat, versus bland, unappetizing food that's nevertheless nutritious. I'd probably pick the food. But then again, what about music that’s actively offensive? Loud, grating noise? The kind of music that makes you want to rip your ears off? Food that actively makes you sick? So, overall, at *its absolute worst*, I'd still probably pick the food. But the difference is close, and it's hard to say, even in theory. The range of potential experience with music is just so massive. And the range of potential experience with food? Well, you can choose to eat the most bland, tasteless food imaginable, but you can also starve.

What movies were marketed in a very misleading way, making the audience expect something different from what was presented? There are a few films that immediately spring to mind, each playing a clever game of bait and switch with the viewing public. One notable example is *Drive*. The trailers for this film, starring Ryan Gosling, heavily emphasized the high-octane action and car chases, painting the picture of a gritty, modern-day heist movie. What audiences actually got, however, was a slow-burn character study with a few bursts of shocking and brutal violence. I recall sitting in the theater, a bit bewildered, as the credits rolled. I wasn't disappointed necessarily – the film is artfully made, dripping with style and simmering tension – but my expectations were undeniably subverted. Then there's *The Witch*, a film that touted itself as a terrifying horror movie. The marketing campaign showed terrifying imagery of the witch, the devil, and creepy goings on, a sort of witch-hunt type film. Though an effective and foreboding film, it moves at a deliberate pace, focusing less on jump scares and more on the psychological disintegration of the family at its center. Some viewers were disappointed, expecting a standard horror film. The true horror of the film relies on the audience’s inability to decipher reality from the slow descent into insanity. Likewise, *Prometheus*, the *Alien* prequel, was marketed as a standalone science fiction epic, a return to the roots of Ridley Scott's original vision. The marketing was deliberately vague on plot details. While certainly sharing some thematic links to *Alien*, *Prometheus* veered into different territory, exploring creation myths, and the origins of humanity. Many expected a more direct connection to the Xenomorphs, and again, felt misled. Ultimately, the effectiveness of this marketing tactic is debatable. Do movies with deceiving trailers attract more viewers initially? Probably. But does it damage audience perception? If, like me, an audience member values the creative freedom displayed by a writer and director to deliver a nuanced cinematic experience, misleading trailers might become more of a nuisance.

What evidence supports the theory of natural selection and evolution as the origin of life on Earth, according to Charles Darwin? Darwin never framed his argument in terms of "the origin of life." He focused on how species change over time – the evolution of existing life – through natural selection. The "origin of life" is a separate question, though it's a question science is chipping away at. As for the evidence for evolution, Darwin's *On the Origin of Species* is a masterclass in marshaling various lines of evidence. First, he looked at the **fossil record**, showing how life forms changed over vast time spans. He noted the similarities and differences between fossils and present-day organisms, indicating a historical progression. Then, he examined **comparative anatomy**: the shared structural features across different species. For instance, the bone structure in a human arm, a whale's flipper, and a bat's wing are remarkably similar, suggesting a common ancestry. Darwin also delved into **embryology**. He observed that developing embryos of diverse species often share common characteristics, such as gill slits, hinting at shared ancestors. **Biogeography** provided another key piece of evidence. Darwin noted that species in geographically close areas are often more similar than species living in similar environments across the globe. This implied species originated somewhere and then spread, adapting to local conditions. Finally, Darwin considered **artificial selection**, observing how humans could breed plants and animals to exhibit specific traits. He argued that if humans could produce such change in a few generations, then nature could, over much longer periods, give rise to the rich diversity of life. These weren't just isolated observations; they formed a cohesive, interlocking argument for the reality of evolution.

Is English considered a foreign language to the US? Why can't most Americans speak English fluently or even close? As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. Why? Well, let's break this down. Technically, no, English isn't a foreign language to the U.S. The U.S. doesn't have an official language at the federal level, but English is the de facto national language. It's what's spoken in most government functions, in schools, and in everyday life. That said, there's no requirement to speak English, and you'll find massive variation in language proficiency across the country. Now, why can't most Americans speak English "fluently" or close? That’s where the waters get murky. Firstly, what does "fluently" even mean? Native speakers don’t need to obsess over perfect grammar or vocabulary. They don’t have to consciously think how to phrase every sentence. They just *know*. So, by some definitions, most Americans *are* fluent, even if they wouldn’t necessarily ace an ESL exam. Secondly, if you mean the ability to speak in perfect or near-perfect English, as taught in schools, that's a different story. American English is a living, ever-evolving organism. Slang, dialects, and regional variations abound, and the “correct” way to speak can be surprisingly flexible. I'm an American, and when I was a teenager, my favorite swear word was "fuck". That's not exactly something you want to bring up in polite company. Finally, many Americans *do* struggle with the complexities of the language. Our education system can be uneven, and English can be a tough language, full of exceptions to the rules. The fact that you've only been learning for three months and feel like you're ahead...well, good for you! Keep it up, and feel proud of your progress. You are definitely ahead of the lazy bums of the world.

What's your go-to healthy snack when cravings hit? As a confirmed snacker, this is a question near and dear to my heart. I’m always on the lookout for a replacement for the chips and cookies that I love but which, let's be honest, don't love me back. First off, the very concept of “healthy” is a minefield in itself, isn’t it? What’s healthy for one person can be a complete disaster for another. But, for the sake of argument, let's define "healthy snacks" as something that has fewer calories, more nutrients, and hopefully, less refined sugar than the usual junk food.  My ideal snack needs a few things. It needs to be easy, convenient, and able to be eaten with one hand (since most of my snacking happens while sitting at my computer). It also needs to deliver some sort of flavor that’s appealing. Frankly, if it tasted like cardboard, I'd be better off just skipping the snack altogether. My current top choice is probably a handful of almonds or walnuts. They're easy to grab, portable, and give that satisfying crunch. They have good fats, are reasonably filling, and they don't leave me feeling guilty afterward. The same goes for a piece of fruit. Apples, oranges, or even a small banana can satisfy a sweet craving. As a bonus, they're easy to eat. I'll also throw in a handful of baby carrots. They have a decent crunch, and something about the blandness is strangely satisfying.

Can airplanes sometimes not store fuel in their tanks due to weight limitations? If this is the case, what are the alternatives for storing fuel in an airplane or other vehicle? Weight considerations are paramount in aircraft design, dictating nearly every aspect, and fuel storage is no exception. Yes, there are situations where airplanes cannot fully utilize their designed fuel tank capacity, particularly in scenarios where maximizing payload or range isn't critical. Often, smaller regional jets or even business jets operate with partially filled tanks for short hops. This lighter load allows for shorter takeoff distances, reduced fuel consumption (ironically!), and increased maneuverability during the flight. So, when faced with such weight limitations, the alternatives for fuel storage become a critical design consideration.  First and foremost, the most common alternative is a reduction in tank size, which, in turn, implies a reduced range capability. Then comes the use of external fuel tanks or drop tanks, which are an option for military aircraft to increase range or ferry range. And, another option is conformal fuel tanks that fit around the fuselage. The more the design pushes for range, the more the overall structure of the aircraft is designed to withstand the stresses imposed on it. If a plane designed to travel great distances is expected to be a workhorse carrying many passengers, the weight becomes more critical than range. Then we get to the overall wing design and the materials involved. With greater stresses, designers are more and more pushed toward lightweight materials, such as composites.

Have you ever gone into a restaurant that looked unappealing from the outside but ended up having delicious food? If so, where and what did you order? Yes! Many times. The most recent example that springs to mind was a little hole-in-the-wall place in a somewhat sketchy part of town. Outside, the building was drab — peeling paint, a faded sign, and a general air of neglect. Honestly, I almost turned around and left, but I was starving and it was the only place nearby. I figured I'd give it a shot. Inside, the decor wasn't much better; it looked like it hadn't been updated since the 70s. But then the food arrived, and I was floored. I ordered the chili verde, and to this day, it's one of the best I've ever had. The meat was tender, the sauce was perfectly spiced, and it came with a generous portion of warm tortillas. The rice and beans were also top-notch, cooked just right. It completely changed my perspective. It taught me not to judge a book by its cover, or, in this case, a restaurant by its facade. There's definitely something to be said for places that focus on what really matters: the food. I’ve had similar experiences with other seemingly unassuming eateries, sometimes a greasy-spoon diner, sometimes a food truck on the side of the road. The lesson always stays the same. Don't be deterred by the outer appearance - it's what's on the plate that matters. I’ve learned the hard way, again and again, that the best culinary experiences often hide in plain sight.

According to the Bible, the earth is only 6000 years old. How does it explain the 4.49-billion-year gap between that and the actual age of the earth? Well, the short answer is: it doesn't. The Bible doesn't attempt to explain the age of the Earth, other than to say that it was created in approximately 6000 years ago. Biblical literalists will often start with that assumption, and then twist the scientific evidence to fit it. This usually takes two forms. The first is denial of carbon dating, or any other scientific technique that contradicts their beliefs, or by claiming that science is fake news. But scientists have come to the same conclusion using many different methods, so that won't cut it. And, I mean, it's quite a stretch to think that almost every scientist, and especially those who are experts in the field, are simply wrong. The second thing they do is cherry pick the science to try to fit their narrative. The classic example is trying to claim that the dinosaurs and humans coexisted (which is simply not true, the dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago), and trying to argue against evolution by natural selection. So, how do they explain the 4.49-billion-year gap? They don't, *really*. They try to sweep it under the rug, or by simply denying the science in the first place. It's not a very convincing argument, and it doesn't withstand any scrutiny. Meanwhile, the scientific evidence for an ancient Earth is overwhelming, and has been verified time and time again by countless independent experiments and observations. So, if somebody tells you that the Earth is only 6000 years old, you can be pretty sure that they either haven't looked at the evidence, or they're deliberately distorting it.

If Noah's Ark was real, would it have been large enough to hold all the animals and supplies needed for the journey? That's the million-dollar question, isn't it? And the answer, when we apply a bit of critical thinking, is a resounding no. Let's break this down, shall we? The Bible tells us the ark was roughly 300 cubits long, 50 cubits wide, and 30 cubits high. Now, a cubit is an ancient unit of measure, and estimates vary, but let's go with roughly 18 inches, or 1.5 feet, for the sake of argument. That gives us an ark about 450 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high. That's not exactly a yacht, but it's still a fairly large vessel. The problem is the sheer number of animals, and the logistical challenges that would present. The Bible mentions "every living thing," which is a pretty broad descriptor, so creationists usually narrow that definition to the "kinds" of animals instead of every single species. Even still, there are some colossal issues. First, there are many animals that couldn't possibly live in the Northern part of the middle east, where all this is said to have occurred , such as polar bears, penguins, and kangaroos. Second, the logistics of obtaining and feeding all these animals, when it's suggested this was done in the first place, is simply beyond reason. You'd need a staff of thousands to handle it all. Then, there's the waste disposal issue. You would need some kind of system for the waste, and while that sort of thing is always glossed over in the story, it still has to be dealt with. Even limiting what we bring, the Ark would have been like a floating zoo, with animals of every variety all crammed together. And finally, what about the food supply? How do you store enough food to feed all those mouths for a year? It's frankly impossible. So, while the story of Noah's Ark is great for Sunday School, the science just doesn't line up.

Hypothetically, let's say there is a world where Christianity is backed by mountains of evidence and all the stories of the Bible are verifiable and proven, would you still follow the teachings of Christianity or choose to live your own life? If I were faced with a world where the tenets of Christianity held up under relentless scrutiny, and every narrative from Genesis to Revelation was undeniably factual, would I embrace the faith or chart my own course? It’s a fascinating thought experiment, one that forces a confrontation with my core beliefs. While I appreciate the philosophical underpinnings of many religions, and I find some of Christianity’s moral guidelines to be sound, such a scenario presents a complex dilemma. It's one thing to *believe*; it's quite another to *know* with absolute certainty. If the evidence were stacked so high as to reach the heavens, and the choice was between verifiable truth and personal autonomy, I'd still lean towards the latter. I value critical thinking. And I believe the freedom to question, to explore, and to define my own path is paramount. If, by some miracle, the Christian God's existence was proven, I wouldn’t abandon my morals and start praying every day out of fear. I'd perhaps view the world with a different lens, understanding its intricacies and embracing the truth, but would still try to adhere to my humanistic principles.

If everyone around the world rides bicycles that generate electricity and store electricity, how much of humanity's electricity consumption can be offset? I'd imagine quite a bit. Okay, let's do some back-of-the-envelope calculations. Worldwide electricity consumption is roughly 23,000 terawatt-hours per year. A terawatt-hour is a billion kilowatt-hours, and a kilowatt-hour is 3.6 megajoules, so that's a lot of energy. Now, most of us sit around all day, so let's say the average person could generate about 100 watts consistently while cycling (that’s pretty reasonable, and some could do way better). Let's estimate that each person, on average, is cycling for around 1 hour per day, and the average person is actually generating electricity for only about 0.5 hours per day (some days we don't cycle, and some days we cycle more, and it's not like all daylight hours are perfect for cycling). So, that's 50 watt-hours of electricity per day. There's roughly 8 billion people on earth, so that is 8,000,000,000 people \* 50 watt-hours/day = 400,000,000,000 watt-hours/day. Now, for a year, that's around 146 terawatt-hours. So, if everyone did that, they'd offset around 0.6% of the world's electricity. Not great, but not nothing either, especially since it's not like it would really cost that much to do. Okay, now let's introduce some more realistic assumptions. It's not like everybody can cycle, and it's not like everyone has access to a bicycle and a device to store electricity. So, let's say that only 10% of people would do this, meaning around 0.06% of the world's electricity consumption could be offset. And there would need to be a huge infrastructure change and a lot of new technology to pull this off. But on the bright side, with enough investment, it's not like it's impossible, or too expensive to do. We already have the technology and the knowledge to build the infrastructure needed to make this a reality. And, more importantly, widespread bicycle riding around the world would bring with it other great benefits, like less pollution and more exercise. So, while the percentage might not be that large, it's still an appealing plan.

If “burger” now includes fish and chicken sandwiches instead of only ground meat patties, what is the boundary between burgers and other sandwiches? This reminds me of the philosophical problem of the heap. If you start removing grains of sand, one at a time, from a pile of sand, at what point does it cease to be a heap? It's a classic, and there's no easy answer. My inclination is that the term "burger" has evolved, and as such, the definition is fluid. It's a matter of cultural acceptance and usage. If enough people use the term to describe a sandwich made with fish or chicken, well, then it *is* a burger. Trying to rigidly define it based on some arbitrary ingredient will be a losing battle. The same holds true for hot dogs. Is a hot dog a sandwich? Many sticklers would say no. It's a hot dog, a category unto itself. But if you put it in a bun, is it really that different from, say, a sub? These are linguistic questions, and the answers are determined by the collective understanding and usage within a community. As long as customers understand what they are purchasing, does it really matter? I suppose if you are running a restaurant and need to categorize things on your menu, a somewhat more formal definition is helpful. But at the end of the day, people either like a thing or they don't. What you call it isn't as important as how it tastes.

If you believe the Bible is fiction, then why would anyone want to write such a work? You know, it's a fair question, and one that gets at the heart of why so many people cling to religious belief even as they struggle with doubts. If you view the Bible as merely a collection of tall tales, as something without any basis in observable reality, then the motivation behind its creation becomes a puzzle. Why would anyone invest so much time, effort, and passion - not to mention, in some cases, their *lives* - in composing something that... well, isn't *true*? You could argue that ancient peoples were simply less sophisticated, prone to believing in anything that sounded remotely plausible. But that explanation falls apart under scrutiny. The level of detail, the complex narratives, the moral teachings woven throughout – all of it suggests a deliberate design, a level of artistry that belies simple naiveté. Some suggest that the Bible was written as a tool to control people, to enforce societal norms through fear and manipulation. And, let's be frank, there's definitely some of *that* in there. But to reduce the entire enterprise to mere social engineering feels, to me, reductive. There's a deeper drive at work, some primal impulse that goes beyond the desire for power. And I think it's probably the same impulse that drives any writer, any artist, or anyone who engages in creative act. The desire to explain the human state, to wrestle with our deepest questions, to give meaning to a chaotic cosmos - it's a way of making sense of the world, a way of fighting back against oblivion.

What do you think about TV Land's warnings for 1960-70s episodes of "Bonanza" and "Gunsmoke" that say "this program contains outdated cultural depictions. Viewer discretion is advised." Do you think this is necessary? Yes, I do think it's necessary, though perhaps not always in the way it's being done. It's the principle I agree with, not necessarily every single execution of it. I mean, those old shows, "Bonanza," "Gunsmoke," all those Westerns and family sitcoms from the 1960s and 70s, they were products of a very different time. And one thing that's clear is that, back then, a lot of things that were considered perfectly acceptable are now, rightly, seen as problematic. Racism, sexism, homophobia, just to name a few. They were baked into the culture, and thus, baked into the TV shows.  So, do I think people should be warned about the outdated cultural depictions? Absolutely. But here’s the thing: these warnings can sometimes come across as a bit… well, sanctimonious. Like the network is patting itself on the back for being so enlightened, while the actual episodes are still there for everyone to watch, problematic content and all. It's a performative form of progressivism, almost. I'd prefer a system where the warnings are more thoughtful and contextualized. Instead of a blanket statement, maybe the warnings could be specific to the episode. "This episode features problematic stereotypes about Native Americans, and viewers may find the language offensive." That way, viewers know exactly what they're getting into, and it allows for an opportunity to use the content as a discussion starter. Frankly, I think the shows themselves are a learning opportunity. They’re a window into the past, a snapshot of the values and biases of a particular era. Watching them, with a critical eye, can be a valuable way to understand how far we've come, and the work that still needs to be done. So, yes, warn people. But also, invite conversation.

Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment? Well, yeah. Seems like there are a few. Firstly, the current technology to generate 80,000 PSI from a single gallon of water is not possible, unless the generator is the size and material of the space station. Secondly, even if that were possible, you’re now left with the question of *how* the energy is generated. And thirdly, even if those two hurdles can be jumped, the energy required to separate hydrogen from water is nothing to sneeze at. You're going to need a lot of energy to do that, way more than any generator powered by a single gallon of water is going to provide. So, you'd have some massive energy loss on the separation end. And you also need to consider a massive amount of infrastructure and equipment. So you'd have a lot of high maintenance equipment at that depth. You'll need specialized equipment, which you'd have to replace deep in the ocean, and lots of it. You'd also need specialized materials that can withstand that immense amount of pressure. Given that even submarines aren't designed to go that far down, the thought experiment seems to be missing quite a few key steps. But, on the other hand, it's theoretically possible to use the energy of the ocean, the hydrogen fuel process does offer quite a bit of energy itself, and the pressure gradient is constant. So there's some things to like too. It's an interesting sci-fi thought experiment! Just needs a bit more technical planning. Maybe a bit of magic, too.

If you are an atheist, how do you explain conscience to yourself? As for YOU, where does it come from? Well, I'm no neuroscientist, so any explanation I give is going to be somewhat simplistic, but I'll give it a shot. The way I see it, our conscience is just another attribute that evolved in the human species. It's a product of our brains, social interactions, and the experiences we've had throughout our lives. Think about it: humans are social animals. We live in groups, rely on each other for survival, and have complex relationships. For a group to function, there needs to be some level of cooperation and a shared understanding of what's right and wrong. So, we evolved a system that encourages helping behavior (and that's the good part), and discourages harmful behavior. That system is what we know as our conscience. It's not some divine voice whispering in our ears, or some objective moral code handed down from on high. Instead, it's a collection of mental processes that leads us to feel guilty when we do something we perceive as wrong, or satisfied (or at least less anxious) when we do something that we (and others) consider good. What about all the different moral codes that exist across different cultures and religions? Well, that's just the natural result of different groups living in different environments and developing different ways of surviving. If you’re surrounded by members of your own tribe who you have a deep personal relationship with, you’re not going to want to hurt them. And with that, there's no need for an all-encompassing moral code. The idea of an all-pervading sense of "love" would mostly be for people you'd never see, or even know. Every moral code is simply a method of promoting social cohesion and preventing the group from tearing itself apart. Now, I know what you're thinking: evolution is "just" a theory, and it’s all just a random process with no underlying meaning. But what is the alternative explanation, that a creator made us to be the way we have always been? That's not really an answer at all. We already know we are made of matter, and are the result of natural processes over the span of billions of years. If you're asking for a "meaning" to life, well, I can't help you there. I don't find the universe has any predetermined meaning, and the sooner you come to terms with that, the better.

Why has Quora devolved into a toxic cesspool? I think there are a few reasons. Quora started off pretty well. In its early days, the questions were interesting, the answers well-written, and there was usually a healthy back-and-forth in the comments. It was like an online salon for the well-informed. But over time, things have changed. One of the biggest factors, I suspect, is that it became too popular. As with anything on the internet, once a site starts getting mainstream attention, it inevitably attracts a different crowd than it was originally tailored for. You start getting the influx of internet trolls whose primary goal seems to be to provoke and belittle, the know-it-alls who can’t help but dominate every conversation, and of course, the spammers looking to exploit the platform. These new users don't care about intelligent discourse or thoughtful answers, they just want to stir things up—or worse still, make a quick buck. Another factor is the shift in the recommendation algorithm. Early on, Quora seemed to reward well-researched and insightful answers. Now it seems to prioritize engagement—the more comments, upvotes, and shares an answer gets, the more visibility it gets. This, unfortunately, incentivizes clickbait questions and sensationalist answers. It also encourages repetitive or derivative content, as those things tend to be what the masses click on most often.
