If you were to squeeze all the empty space out of all the atoms that make up a human, they'd take up about the size of sugar cube. And, I'm sitting here typing on a computer that's also mostly empty space. So, if these random arrangements can happen, it means that the specific arrangements needed for life, and even civilization, are not theoretically impossible. But it really does depend on what you mean by life. If you're looking for single-cell organisms, even bacteria, it seems that those are fairly common throughout the universe. We've found them in environments on Earth that were previously thought to be uninhabitable, and there’s good circumstantial evidence that they may exist on other planets. In this case, the odds of life are very good. As you move up the chain of existence, to things that resemble complex organisms, or animals, the odds of life get steadily worse. And if you're looking for intelligent, tool-using species capable of things like writing blog posts and Quora answers, then the odds get much, much worse. You have to consider all sorts of things for complex life, but this is beyond the scope of the question. It's not only the physical parameters: like, the Earth has to be at the exact right distance from its star for liquid water to exist. But, you also need to consider the planet’s geology. Does your planet have tectonic plates and a magnetic field, which help to regulate climate and act as a shield against solar radiation? And as your species becomes more advanced, you have to consider the social parameters. Can they cooperate for the common good, or will they just blow themselves up with their technology (much like we’ve been flirting with over the past century?) There’s something called the Fermi Paradox, which relates to this topic. The basic idea is that the Universe is gigantic, very old, and has plenty of stars and planets that could, in theory, be home to life. So, why haven’t we encountered any other intelligent species? Anyway, I don't know how to quantify the odds of any of this with any real precision. But from where I'm sitting, I can only conclude that the odds of life are extremely low. And the odds of intelligent life are even lower. But, it only takes one planet to go from theoretical to actual.

Is reheating leftovers in a microwave good or bad? I'm no food scientist, that's for sure. But while I don't know if nuking last night's dinner is objectively "good" or "bad," I do have some thoughts. First, let's acknowledge the sheer convenience of the contraption. Sure, there are those who insist on the oven or stovetop. I get it: crispier textures, more even heating, the whole shebang. But when you're staring into the abyss of a mountain of dishes and a looming work deadline, the microwave becomes a siren song. Plop that Tupperware in, hit a few buttons, and boom, you're back in the game. And let's also admit it: sometimes, the food *does* taste better microwaved, sometimes better than it did the first time. The last time I had a pizza, half of it I ate and saved the other half for the next day, and heated it up in the microwave. I don't know what it is, but pizza is almost always still fantastic when reheated in that way. But then, a good pizza is almost always fantastic in general. But, you know, there's probably a lot of variables on that. Anyway, I can't help but wonder if science is all that settled on the microwave being safe anyway. I mean, it's not the 1950s anymore, but the principles it uses are so weird, and I wonder what long-term effects are. I'll probably continue eating out of it as long as it's working, but definitely something I'll keep an eye on over the years. After doing a quick search of the subject I did find a bunch of things to watch out for, such as plastic containers possibly leaching chemicals into your food. That I knew, and that makes total sense to me. And I do try to be conscious of that when I'm using the microwave, but I admit I'm not perfect, I just try. Either way, I'd say microwaves are pretty practical, and I don't think they're going anywhere.

If Christianity is wrong, then why do people believe in it? This is, of course, a valid question. Plenty of things that aren't true are widely believed, especially in any area where there's no easy way to prove something objectively. But, in many ways, the question is a bit loaded, because if the question were, "If *any* religion is wrong," then that would be an even better question. I mean, I'm inclined to believe the same reasons that lead people to believe in Christianity also lead people to believe in Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, etc. And if you want to take the question at a different level, you could ask, "If *any* conspiracy theory is wrong, then why do people believe in it?" The basic answer to all these questions comes down to a combination of the human need to believe, and the human tendency to believe things that comfort us, explain the world, and/or fit the pattern that's already established in our brains. Let's examine that, because the reasons why people believe in these things, and the reasons why people *keep* believing in these things, aren't exactly the same. Obviously, the reasons why the first Christian believed aren't necessarily the same reasons why a Christian today *continues* to believe. First, the original reasons... In a modern context, people often get introduced to religion via their parents. Usually, the kids adopt the same belief, and since they're children, they don't have the ability to deeply question any of it. As they get older, and the idea of Hell is still in the back of their mind, they realize they can't *really* prove that their parents were wrong. That's a big part of how the belief gets established in the first place. But there are other reasons. I mean, for a young person, the Bible contains a lot of fun stories, has some nice guidance on how to live your life, and, yes, even some helpful moral teachings.

Why is there so much debate over the math question 12÷2(2+4) =? It's funny that you ask this question, because I think it's a perfect example of why math education in the U.S. is so lacking. As you can see from the other answers, the math itself isn't hard, involving only the simplest of operations: addition, multiplication, and division. The source of the controversy has to do with conventions. A mathematical equation, like any language, has a set of rules to clarify it. To oversimplify a bit, these rules are: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication and Division, Addition and Subtraction. In this case, the only ambiguity comes from the multiplication and division operations, which are of equal precedence. Operations of equal precedence are solved in order from left to right, unless the operations are explicitly grouped by parentheses. So a properly written equation would be: 12 ÷ [2(2+4)] = ? or (12÷2)(2+4) = ? And now, with the ambiguity removed, the answers are easy. Now, back in the real world, in the absence of properly written equations, math teachers are often forced to teach some rule of thumb like PEMDAS in order to get every student to arrive at a correct answer. Most students will memorize the rule, while even fewer will bother to learn why the rule works. It also doesn't help the student to be told “just follow the steps” without explaining the math behind it. Math education is not designed to prepare you for future math classes; it is also designed to try to help students think logically, something that is useful in any profession or job. So, it is really not surprising that there's so much confusion, particularly among people who haven't taken a math class in a long time. It's also not surprising that there's a lot of passionate debate about these types of questions. This leads me to believe there's a market for these types of problems, and they probably are just designed to generate clicks and comments. I mean, if you already know what the answer is, great, fine. But, if you don’t, and you’re interested, then there’s a lot to learn. You can delve deeper into mathematical notation and the logic of solving equations. And even better, try finding this out for yourself. Don’t just take somebody’s word for it.

How was the 2024 solar eclipse? Was there much of a panic/emergency as the USA prepared for or just a fizzle? I'm in Texas, and I can tell you that the eclipse was spectacular. I was fortunate enough to experience totality, and it was an absolutely unforgettable experience, a moment of awe and wonder that I'll carry with me for the rest of my days. The sky went dark; stars appeared. People screamed in excitement, like they were cheering a final goal. The corona was visible. I'm not sure if the other states were quite as lucky because the weather wasn't cooperating, but I'm so glad the skies cleared here. As for a panic, or an emergency: no. The weeks leading up to the eclipse were filled with a lot of hype, sure, but the government and local officials seemed pretty well prepared. There were warnings to stay safe, to wear eclipse glasses, to stock up on gas and groceries, but it was all rather matter-of-fact. There was a lot of traffic, and hotel rooms booked up quickly, but nothing out of the ordinary for a major event. I saw some traffic alerts, but there were also a bunch of people lining the sides of the highway watching the event, and there weren't any major crashes. I'm sure the emergency services were on alert, but everything went pretty smoothly. So, the eclipse was an amazing success. The only real fizzle was, as with many things in life, the hype leading up to it.

What is the science behind a ouija board? Has anyone ever had an experience that made them question reality? Boy, isn't it funny that people believe a piece of cardboard and a plastic planchette can communicate with the dead? I mean, sure it's entertaining for stories, and horror movies have made a killing off them (pun absolutely intended). But seriously, let's get real: it's just a game, right? Anyone who tells you otherwise is either pulling your leg or, and I say this with a grain of salt, has way too much time on their hands. As for the science, or rather, the lack thereof, behind the Ouija board, it's all down to the ideomotor effect. Basically, your subconscious is making tiny, nearly imperceptible movements. You *think* you're not pushing that little plastic thing, but believe me, you are. Your brain, without you even realizing it, is guiding the planchette to spell out those thrilling, spooky messages. It's the same principle behind things like dowsing rods, or those "psychic" tests where they claim to be reading your mind by watching your body language; even those silly "fortune tellers" that claim to tell you your future. And the experience that makes you question reality? Well, that's a tricky one. I've had plenty of experiences where I questioned things, but it was from things like bad food. But as for anything truly paranormal? Nope. No ghosts, no demons, and certainly no Ouija board revelations. But what about all the "stories" you hear, all the tales of things that are not able to be explained by science? Well, people like to tell stories. Some of them are even true. Others… not so much. And when you're dealing with something so open to suggestion as a Ouija board, memory bias, confirmation bias, and that good old-fashioned human tendency to see patterns where there often aren’t any? You get all kinds of spooky stories.

I totally believe the evolution theory because it has tons of scientific evidence, but I don't get it how marine life evolved to have lungs, limbs, developed, and somehow intelligent brain to live on land? You know, I've thought about that very question, and it's a fascinating one. The transition from aquatic life to terrestrial existence is undoubtedly a complex, multi-stage process. There isn't a single "aha!" moment where a fish sprouted legs and walked ashore. Instead, it was a gradual series of adaptations, each providing a survival advantage in a changing environment. Think about it: a fin that's slightly sturdier, enabling a creature to prop itself up on the shallows. A lung, or lung-like structure, that supplements oxygen intake in oxygen-poor waters. A brain that enables coordination and the ability to navigate a different terrain. These were advantageous traits that, over vast stretches of time, were amplified through natural selection. The fossil record provides a wealth of transitional forms that illuminate this history. We can see the gradual development of limbs, the repositioning of eyes, and the structural changes in skulls and jaws. There are intermediary species showing these changes which is fascinating to study. It's not like there's a gaping hole in the scientific understanding, but rather continuous, evolving evidence. And about intelligence: I think our understanding of it's development is still in an early stage. Intelligence, or cognition, is itself a kind of adaptation, one that allows living beings to find food, avoid danger and reproduce, and that has evolved in numerous forms over the course of life. These aren't instant transformations, but the result of minuscule changes over the course of millions of years. It’s a truly powerful testament to the workings of evolution.

Atheists who talk about how morality is about "empathy" & act as if that`s an universal fact, why the ego? Literally evil isn`t cosmical. And unless one cares for the subjective goal (in this case well-being) there is nothing really wrong with harm. Look, I'm all for empathy, and I agree that it has an important role to play in morality. Empathy is, I think, the basis for a lot of our moral feelings, as it allows us to understand (or at least imagine) the suffering of other people. So I wouldn't say it's *wrong* to talk about empathy. But I also think it's an oversimplification to say that empathy *is* morality, or that it's the *only* source of morality, or that it's universally shared. It certainly *can* be useful to discuss morality in terms of empathy, as it can help us, as a society, to come to some sort of agreement on ethical issues. For example, if one can get most people to agree on the fact that needless suffering is bad, then you can make some progress on animal rights and other issues. But empathy doesn't get you all the way. Many people are perfectly willing to inflict suffering on others, either in self-defense, or to advance their own interests, or because they're part of some group that's in conflict with another group. There are plenty of cases in which empathy breaks down, either because people are actively trying to harm others, or because they don't understand the plight of people who have different experiences. And that's where it gets tricky. Because, at the individual level, what "well-being" even means is going to vary from person to person, and from culture to culture. For example, some people get a sense of well-being from sacrificing a lot of their own, personal pleasure to get something from a higher power. Others, not so much. So it's perfectly possible for two different people to have contradictory ideas about what counts as a good moral course of action. And if someone's moral compass doesn't necessarily point toward what I consider to be "right", well, that's also a problem.

Has a company ever done something so annoying that you swore off ever buying any of their products ever again? Oh, absolutely, several times, in fact. It doesn’t happen on a daily basis, but every so often, a company manages to irk me to such a degree that I make a conscious decision to sever ties. I'm even willing to pay more for a competitor's product. One instance that immediately springs to mind involved a prominent electronics manufacturer whose customer service was, to put it charitably, abysmal. I won't name the specific company, but let's just say their name rhymes with "Apple." I was having a minor issue with a newly purchased device–nothing catastrophic, just a glitch that needed troubleshooting. After a considerable amount of wasted time on hold – the hold music was an offense to my ears, filled with overly upbeat elevator-style tunes – and a series of frustrating interactions with their support staff, who seemed to be reading off a script without any understanding of the actual problem, I just gave up. The whole experience left me apoplectic, and convinced me to switch brands, even if the alternative wasn’t quite as sleek or feature-rich. Then there was a time with a clothing retailer who inexplicably decided to send me marketing emails every single day, despite my repeated attempts to unsubscribe. I tried every trick in the book, but the emails just kept coming. It was clearly a deliberate ploy, bordering on harassment. So, I went cold turkey. There's no amount of snazzy marketing or discounts that will ever get me to buy anything from them again. Small annoyances? I can deal with those - a few of them. But outright contempt for the customer's time and attention? That's a surefire way to lose my business.

Why did Tim Walz put female tampons and pads in the boys washroom? I haven't followed this particular story closely, so I can't comment on the specifics of the situation. However, I can say that the reactions have been predictably polarized, with the predictable outrage from some, and the equally predictable support from others. To be honest, though, the whole issue, while not unimportant, is still pretty minor in the grand scheme of things. I mean, the government is making decisions about global warming and wars, and this kind of stuff gets more attention? I'm not saying it's *un*-important: certainly, I don't want my taxes to be used on things that are actively harmful. But to get this worked up over tampons and pads is a sign that there are other more meaningful things to be done.

Do atheists believe that cucumbers could evolve into kangaroos if given enough time? No, that's not something I've ever heard an atheist posit. It's more the opposite, actually. I would expect that atheists, being believers in evolution, would be more likely to understand the time that's necessary for some species to evolve into others.* Though, I'm not sure where the idea of cucumbers somehow evolving into kangaroos would come from in the first place. While it’s true that evolution can produce a wide variety of life forms, that doesn't mean that just anything can evolve into anything else, and a cucumber is not on the path to becoming a kangaroo. At least, I'd be extremely surprised to see that occur. Also, the question itself sounds suspiciously like something a creationist might ask. And I'm not one to shy away from a good debate with a creationist. I already presented my opinions about these folks in previous paragraphs, but let me clarify. I don't think I've ever met a creationist who wasn’t sincere in their beliefs (unlike the flat-earthers), so I typically won't say anything to them unless they directly ask me about it. However, if they bring their beliefs to my doorstep, then all bets are off, and I’ll happily engage. *And I'm not even saying this just to try to win them over to my side. I think, at this point, I've accepted most of them. And I think they've accepted me.* But, as an atheist, I'm very much aligned with mainstream evolutionary science. And speaking of evolution, that brings me to another point that I was thinking about. Why are there so many different animals? Why aren't they all evolving into people, or at least trying to be more people-like? And the answer to that is that there's no need. Every different animal type is adapted to a different niche in the environment. They're already doing just fine.

What percents of people do and don’t support abortion? I'm an atheist, and I have no fondness for abortion. I support it in many situations. What gives? Well, it's all about circumstances, right? To clarify, I am decidedly pro-choice, but I don't *like* abortion. If abortion were somehow eliminated from the planet tomorrow, I wouldn't shed a tear, and I'd celebrate that a difficult and sometimes tragic option had been removed. But, in the real world, it is a necessary evil. In many cases, it is the better of two bad options, or the only option available. So let's look at the different circumstances that might affect the abortion issue. First off, let's consider a pregnancy that is wanted by both parents, and that is viable. This is the ideal situation, and in this case, I am obviously against abortion. But unfortunately, it is not always the case. Next off, let's consider a pregnancy that is unwanted by both parents. Maybe it arose out of a one-night stand, or a drunken mistake. Or perhaps the couple is poor and can't afford a kid right now. As long as they are responsible, and don't plan to just abandon a baby, I'd still advocate for abortion or adoption. Again, adoption is ideal (giving a baby to loving parents), but it's not always realistic. Sometimes abortion is the most responsible option. Then there are the really hard cases. What if the mother is suffering from a life-threatening illness? Or what if the pregnancy arose out of rape or incest? Some of the worst cases are prenatal diagnosis that reveals a severe genetic defect. As for rape, I am not one of these "only in case of rape or incest" pro-choicers. If it's a wanted pregnancy, even if the pregnancy arose out of rape or incest, abortion is not the best choice. But of course, many women might rightfully choose abortion in this case. Even if it's not a moral decision, it is a human decision, and this is why it has to be legal. As to hard cases with severe genetic defects, these are the ones that really make me sad. I have a friend who went through this situation, and I offered my support. Ultimately, it's their decision, but it's a tough one. So how do these feelings play out in society? Well, even though I have strong pro-choice views, these feelings are really nuanced, and that probably sums up society in general.

Why are non-professional cyclists drawn to road bikes? A number of factors conspire to lure folks toward the sinuous curves and high-performance design of road bikes, even if they're not gunning for the yellow jersey. Firstly, there's the siren song of speed. Road bikes are engineered for efficiency, optimized for slicing through the wind with their drop bars and narrow tires. Casual riders, even if they aren't chasing Strava segments, appreciate the feeling of effortless velocity. Then there's the aesthetic appeal. Let's be frank: They look cool. The sleek lines, the minimalist design, the way a good road bike just seems to *flow* down the street—it's a visual treat. It's a statement, proclaiming to the world that you appreciate form as much as function. Beyond that, cycling, at its core can be a very efficient form of exercise. Road bikes, with their light weight and responsive handling, make that exercise as enjoyable possible. And for those who commute or run errands by bike, a road bike can make a big difference in the ease of distance, and the ability to cover more ground without undue fatigue. The versatility is appealing, especially for those who also enjoy exploring. You can comfortably cycle any distance, from a quick spin around the block to a century ride through the countryside. However, it probably wasn't a bike shop professional that got you hooked. A friend, coworker, or even a family member likely got you started. So, in short, there's the allure of speed, the sleek appearance, the effective workout benefit, and the practicality – all of which explain the enduring appeal of the road bike.

Would you rather be stranded on an island with 100 right wingers or 100 left wingers, and why? Well, this is a fun thought experiment, and I think the answer is pretty obvious. I’d rather be stranded with 100 left wingers. Now, before all the right-wingers get their knickers in a twist, let me explain. The key isn't just the political viewpoint, though that’s certainly a factor. The key is whether the people are likely to cooperate, and whether they’re likely to have valuable skills. I mean, stranded on an island? You’d need people who can build shelter, find water, start a fire, hunt for food, maybe even build a boat if you want a shot at getting off the island. And you need people who can work together efficiently – who are going to try compromise and collaboration, instead of always trying to score points against the other side. Now, I know this is stereotyping a bit, but in general, I'd guess that left-leaning people would have more of these skills and be better at working together.

If Trump wasn’t on the ballot how would the democrats hide stealing democracy from the people by handing the nomination to Kamala w/o the vote of the people? Why is Biden allowed to appoint his successor? That’s a loaded question, isn't it? The premise itself is rather… suspect. The idea that the Democrats are somehow *hiding* anything, especially the alleged "stealing" of democracy, presupposes a level of organized malfeasance that would be breathtaking in its scope and complexity. Frankly, it would require a conspiracy of epic proportions, involving countless people at various levels of power, all maintaining absolute secrecy. And for what? To ensure Kamala Harris gets the nomination? It's not like she's some unknown quantity—she's been a prominent figure for years. It's a bit like suggesting that the sun will rise in the west, and the Democrats are somehow behind that too. As for Biden appointing his successor, that’s not how it works. Presidential nominations are decided by the people, whether through primaries and caucuses, the party convention, or, in extreme cases, possibly the party's National Committee. There's no provision for a sitting president to just anoint someone. The question itself is more a statement of belief in a conspiracy theory than a genuine inquiry.

If in the USA we have freedom of press, why is it legal for social media to control what we can and can not post? That's a genuinely excellent question, and one that I've been mulling over myself lately. The crux of the issue, I suppose, lies in the distinction between the First Amendment and the legal framework governing private entities like social media platforms. Freedom of the press, as it's enshrined in the Constitution, acts as a shield against governmental censorship. The government isn't supposed to dictate what traditional news outlets, or individuals, can write or say (with the caveat that there are limits, such as libel laws). However, social media companies aren't exactly "the press", at least not in the Founding Fathers' minds. They're private businesses. They aren't the government. They're like a private town square, and they have a right to set the rules of engagement within their own little fiefdoms. They're not legally obligated to host any content whatsoever. Think of it like this: Your house is your domain. You're free to invite anyone you like over, and to tell anyone you don't like to get lost. You can establish standards of conduct for your dinner parties, or ban certain topics of conversation. Same deal with Facebook, Twitter, etc. They have their own rules and regulations, and you have to play by them if you want to use their platform. Now, don't get me wrong, this doesn't mean there aren't legitimate concerns here. The power wielded by these social media giants is immense, and if they are arbitrarily silencing voices or displaying bias, that can cause great problems, and is something that should be guarded against. But in a society governed by law, it's complicated. It's something that definitely needs nuanced evaluation, but the answer isn't as simple as declaring a violation of freedom of the press.

Is the platypus related to dinosaurs or birds in terms of evolution? No, the platypus is not directly related to dinosaurs or birds, and it's a bit more complex than that. This is another great example of how evolution works, and a missed opportunity to educate those "lucky 10,000" people who are about to learn something new. Dinosaurs were reptiles, so they're more closely related to modern-day reptiles, birds, and mammals than to the platypus – even though, of course, there's still the same distant common ancestry. But, platypuses are monotremes, which means they're mammals that lay eggs, a very primitive trait. And that's the key. The platypus has only a handful of relatives: the echidnas. These monotremes split off from the rest of the mammals very early in the mammalian evolutionary tree, even before the marsupials like kangaroos, or placental mammals like humans, whales, and dogs. In other words, the platypus is more distantly related to us than other mammals, reptiles, birds, or dinosaurs. Their ancestors started diverging from the rest of the mammals *way* back in the time of the dinosaurs. So if you really want to put it in terms of evolution, the monotremes, reptiles, birds, and dinosaurs don't even share a direct common 'ancestor'. They're very distantly related, and the monotremes are even more distantly related. That difference makes the platypus such a strange-looking creature. And that also means they could be considered "living fossils," retaining many more of the traits of ancient mammals than the overwhelming majority of their mammal cousins. They have a bill and webbed feet like a duck, a venomous spur like a reptile, and lay eggs like a bird, while also sharing the classic traits of a mammal: fur and production of milk. They're a true mish-mash of features, a testament to how evolution can produce such interesting and varied results.

What are the units of Einstein’s mass energy equivalence equation E=mc^2? If E were in Joules what would m be? If m were in ng what would E be? Or is there some weird mathematical black magic that makes the units completely unrelatable to normies? Good question. Let's break this down, since the units in Einstein's most famous equation, E=mc², can be a bit baffling at first glance.  *   **E is Energy**: Energy is measured in Joules (J). Think of it as the capacity to do work. *   **m is Mass**: Mass is measured in kilograms (kg). This is a measure of how much "stuff" an object contains. *   **c is the Speed of Light:** This is a constant value, approximately 299,792,458 meters per second (m/s).  So the equation *technically* looks like this: J = kg \* (m/s)². And to answer your more specific questions:  *   **If E is in Joules, then m is in Kilograms.** The equation is set up so that if you use standard units (Joules for energy, kilograms for mass, and meters per second for the speed of light — which you always must use), everything works out. *   **For mass in ng:** Alright, now you're getting crafty. If m is in nanograms (ng), then E would be in Joules. The conversion factor to use is 1 ng = 1 x 10-12 kg. So, to use the equation you'd have to multiply the speed of light squared and the mass *in kilograms*. Therefore, even if you measure the mass in nanograms, the energy that comes out is still in Joules.  And no, there's no "black magic." The units are all related, and this conversion is just simple algebra, following the rules of math we all learned... or maybe forgot in high school. It's all based on what we've observed about the physical world. The core idea is that mass and energy are related, and the equation shows you how much energy is equivalent to a given amount of mass, and vice versa. The speed of light is a very big number, so multiplying the mass (in kg) by the speed of light squared gives you a very large amount of energy (in J). That conversion, the relationship between mass and energy, is, in my opinion, one of the coolest things in all of physics.

If you die, is there anything you can do to leave lasting evidence that you have left traces and existed on the earth forever? Well, that's a fascinating question that's simultaneously profound and a touch morbid. Honestly, the idea of leaving behind some tangible proof of your existence, some enduring mark after you're gone, is something that likely crosses everyone’s mind at some point. It's a very human desire, this yearning for some form of immortality, and the fear of being completely erased from memory. Now, can you *actually* leave lasting evidence, something that will remain untouched by time? That's a tough one. You can certainly create things that *might* last a while – write a book, compose music, build a house, have children, contribute to scientific discoveries, etc. – but all those things are subject to decay, obsolescence, and the whims of fate. The house may crumble, the music may be forgotten, the book may be lost, your descendants might not remember you. However, you could also look at the bigger picture. Everything's made of atoms, and those atoms never truly disappear. So, in a sense, your physical matter will become part of the earth and the universe, recycled into new forms. A bit of a consolation prize, maybe? It's not like folks will be able to point at a specific star and say, "There's a bit of that guy!" But the energy you once embodied will continue to exist. Ultimately, though, I think the most lasting impact you can have is on other people. The way you treat them, the lessons you teach, the love you share – those things can live on in the memories and actions of others. It's the intangible that endures, the ripple effect you create in the world.

Why do other religions think that Catholics worship 3 gods? I'm not entirely sure where this comes from. Catholics are pretty upfront that they only believe in one God, the same God worshipped by Jews and Muslims. I suspect the confusion comes from the doctrine of the Holy Trinity – God the Father, God the Son (Jesus), and God the Holy Spirit – and the fact that Catholics pray to saints (important people in the religion's history). However, at least in theory, these are all just aspects of one God. It might not be a perfect comparison, but it's somewhat similar to saying that the United States has three branches of government. Only a non-American (or maybe a confused American) might say that the U.S. has three governments. And while Catholics certainly venerate saints, and ask for them to intercede on their behalf, they’re clearly not considered gods. They’re more akin to asking a friend or family member to pray for (or help) you. I suppose religions like Hinduism have multiple gods, but they don’t seem to me to be anything like the Catholic belief system. In summary, it may be a misunderstanding, and it may be some sort of bad faith accusation. But whatever the situation, it's incorrect. I find that those people rarely understand the religion they're criticizing, and don't want to.

How does an atheist explain 1 cor 15 appearance to the 12 stated by Paul, who investigated and interacted with them directly? This is a difficult question for me to answer, because it depends on what you mean by "explain" and what you mean by "appearance." The Christian interpretation is that at the same time that the resurrected Jesus was seen by Mary Magdalene, as described in the gospels, he was also seen by his disciples, which led to the initial spread of Christianity. As an atheist, I don't believe that Jesus was actually resurrected and appeared before anyone. So instead, I can only offer speculative explanations or a more pragmatic view. If what you want is a historical explanation, then the best answer is that historians aren't sure what happened. We have the writings of Paul that claim that the disciples saw a resurrected Jesus, but we don't have anything besides that to corroborate it (and even Paul didn't witness it firsthand - he claims it was revealed to him). In his letters, Paul may not have been interested in documenting the event, or the event may not have been as crucial to him as his theology. So, the fact that we don't know what happened doesn't bother me. The fact that someone may believe something, and claim it happened, doesn't make it true. If the "appearance" was a hallucination, or a legend that was expanded over the years, or a deliberate lie, then those are all possibilities that could be the basis for a historical explanation. Another possibility is that Paul and the disciples did experience something and believed it, but the event was misrepresented over the centuries. In other words, the fact that an event "happened" doesn't necessarily mean that it happened the way Christians believe it.

Why do atheists put gods from polytheistic religions alongside the Abrahamic one as if they're equal? Polytheism is impossible because separate realities or existences are impossible. There can only be one god. Well, this is a very interesting point, and I think the distinction between monotheism and polytheism does need some unpacking. The core of the issue, as I see it, stems from the inherent claim to exclusivity that monotheistic religions often assert. They typically posit the existence of *the* one true God, which, by definition, renders all other gods, or any other kind of supernatural entity, false. Polytheistic religions, on the other hand, don't necessarily make such claims. They can coexist, and often do, with other pantheons of gods and spirits. To be clear, I'm personally an atheist, and so I reject the existence of *all* gods, whether singular or plural but with no claim of exclusivity. But if you're going to assess the claims made by various religions about reality, I think the specific structure of each belief system is relevant. It's like comparing apples and oranges, or comparing apples and the color red. You have an organized, cohesive system, versus a collection of, well, anything else. So when atheists compare monotheistic gods to polytheistic gods, it's not a matter of treating them "as if they're equal." It's often more about highlighting that *both* are supernatural entities. Both are not empirically verifiable. Both exist only inside belief systems. And in my mind, all lack any substantial evidence and are therefore, equally unconvincing. It's like arguing over which fictional character is the most powerful. It's all fantasy, the power levels are whatever the writers or believers want them to be. So, from an atheist's perspective, the number of gods isn't the crucial distinction. It's the lack of any real-world evidence to support any divine claims that creates the problem. The same way that the validity of a scientific theory does not depend on how many scientists accept it. The proof is the proof, not the popularity.

What is the reasoning behind atheists thinking it's illogical to believe in god? Should people be allowed to have their own beliefs without being challenged by others? The reasoning behind atheist skepticism is varied, but a common thread is a lack of compelling evidence. The absence of proof, for many, is the primary reason for disbelief. The burden of proof, they argue, lies with those making the extraordinary claim of a divine being. Furthermore, atheists often find the concept of a god—or multiple competing gods—logically inconsistent, pointing to paradoxes, contradictions, and the problem of evil as stumbling blocks to rational acceptance. Regarding the second question, the ideal of a tolerant society allows for diverse viewpoints. The rub lies in how those beliefs manifest. People absolutely should be free to hold whatever beliefs they want in their own minds. However, when those beliefs lead to demonstrable harm, discrimination, or the suppression of others' rights and freedoms, then I think it is more than acceptable to push back. I would add that even *without* harm, I think it is perfectly fine to politely question or discuss beliefs. It's the same with any other topic. But in the end, everyone should have a right.

Is a ruler exactly 12 inches? Surely if you zoom in trillions and trillions and trillions of times, then the length of the ruler has to be ever so slightly different than exactly 12 inches, correct? Well, it depends on what we mean by "exactly." If we're talking about mathematics, then, yes, it is impossible for a ruler to be *exactly* 12 inches because real-world objects are never perfectly precise. Even the most carefully crafted ruler will have minute variations at the atomic level. But, in the context of everyday life, the answer is different, and in most real-world situations, it's perfectly fine to say the ruler is exactly 12 inches. Unless you are doing something in a lab where you need to measure exactly the size of an atom or something. In those cases, the word "exactly" becomes a lot fuzzier. But generally speaking, even an exceptionally cheap ruler will be close enough for most purposes. You're probably not going to notice the difference if you, for example, are building a bookshelf. And that's all that really matters. Now, if we bring in quantum physics, things get even more bizarre. The simple act of observing the ruler with a measuring tool would, in itself, alter the ruler, however slightly. It's the observer effect, so the mere act of measuring something changes it, which in the case of a ruler makes the word "exactly" even more difficult to define. So, is the ruler exactly 12 inches? It depends on what kind of exactness you are looking for.

What do atheists do on Christmas Day? Honestly, not much different than anyone else, I imagine. Christmas Day is a cultural holiday in the U.S., and I’ll readily participate in the cultural aspects, even if the religious aspects don’t really apply to me. I mean, Santa Claus is a fun tradition even if you don’t believe in, well, Santa Claus. We atheists are not the Grinch who stole Christmas. We still enjoy presents, good food, family, and the overall festive mood. My Christmas Day will probably involve waking up, opening presents with my wife and kids, eating a big breakfast, and then relaxing. We'll likely visit family and friends and maybe watch a Christmas movie later in the evening. So in short, we do pretty much what everyone else does. Now, with that said, some of the religious aspects can be a bit strange to me. For example, I often get asked if I think the nativity story is “beautiful”. Well, I can certainly recognize that it’s part of human culture, and its influence on Western Civilization is undeniable. But I have zero belief in supernatural events, so, no, I can’t say I find the story particularly “beautiful” in the sense that it portrays actual events. And, similarly, I'm not a fan of the religious hymns. But that's a small price to pay to enjoy the holiday. So, to sum up my position: We're happy to partake in the secular, non-religious traditions. We can't really be expected to be enthusiastic about the religious aspects, but we're not going to begrudge anyone their beliefs.

What is the belief of atheists regarding the value of all life, including unborn fetuses? Since atheists don't believe in a god, and thus have no religious doctrine dictating the inherent value of life, the answer to this question can be stated fairly simply: Atheists value all life, including unborn fetuses, to varying degrees. As in, the same way that anybody else values all life to varying degrees. Now, if you ask about specific arguments, I can certainly address that: For the vast majority of atheists (though I don't speak for all!), valuing all life is a simple matter of empathy. We only get to experience this life once, so it’s pretty tragic to see any life snuffed out, be it a human, deer, or insect. Also, as a species, we've become incredibly reliant on our fellow humans to provide services and a support network, so murdering people is generally taken by those who aren't sociopaths to be a bad thing. And when it comes to fetuses, they're not people yet, but they have the potential to become people. Most of us are against needlessly ending lives, so most atheists are against aborting viable fetuses (though, as I noted, that can vary by individual). That's all there is to it. As an aside, I find it amusing how often believers in a god ask atheists moral questions. It's almost as though they think we have no moral code without religion. But I think our morals are pretty good, and even better in some ways. We don't get any of that "Well, God *said* to kill them" justification for bad behavior.

According to Newton's 2nd law, F=ma, but when we push the wall, why does it not accelerate? When you push the wall, the wall pushes back. It’s a lesson in equilibrium, a dance of forces that cancels each other out. Newton’s 3rd law, to every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction, dictates this. You're applying a force to the wall, certainly, but the wall is, in turn, applying an equal and opposite force back onto you. So while F=ma holds true, it does not directly tell the whole story of the wall's behavior. The net force on the wall is zero. If the net force is zero, there's no acceleration to be seen. If you were to push an object in a vacuum with no other forces acting on it, *then* it would accelerate per the 2nd law. But in the real world, forces are almost always in constant, mutual tension. You're not just dealing with the force *you're* applying. You're also dealing with other forces acting on it as well. Think about it like a tug-of-war, where the wall and you are on opposite sides, and it is the ground that is the anchor keeping you from moving the wall. Both you and the wall are locked in a static battle. So, the wall is perfectly happy to remain at rest, resisting your efforts. The same isn't true of a shopping cart. As you push the cart in the grocery store, now the forces are unbalanced. Your force overpowers the friction from the wheels. This is why the cart moves. And for a fun thought experiment, if you had the ability to apply limitless force to the wall, *then* the wall would begin to accelerate.
